about: How well human professional fortune tellers actually scored on these exact questions. Transcribed from the organizer's published results. This is a real human baseline: entrants were practising masters competing publicly under their own names for a trophy, on questions whose answers were sealed until after the contest closed.
caveats: Only the top finishers' scores are published. The mean over all entrants is not known for any edition, so these numbers are a ceiling, not an average.

Entrant counts are not published for most editions, so the ceiling is not comparable across editions: a top score drawn from 200 entrants is a higher-order statistic than the same score drawn from 20.

From the 9th edition on, the official ranking is not the raw score. The rule is diving-style: each entrant's best-scoring case and worst-scoring case are dropped, leaving the middle six cases (30 of 40 questions). Both figures are given below where published; `raw` is the one comparable to running a model over all items in this dataset.

A consequence the organizer states outright on the 2022 sheet: the highest raw total is not necessarily the champion. In 2022 the best raw score, 21/40, belonged to a runner-up. `best_raw_overall` records the highest raw score published for an edition regardless of who placed where — that is the figure to compare a model against.
Editions differ in option count, so the random-guess baseline differs (see `random_baseline`).

For 2022–2025 the questions in this dataset come via MingLi-Bench while these scores are transcribed from the organizer's own tables — two independent sources. Three of those four editions have a primary answer sheet and were audited item by item (scripts/crosscheck_vendor.py); 2025 has none.

The per-case breakdowns published for 2023 and 2024 are parenthesised as (2:n)…(9:n) — eight cases numbered 2 through 9, not 1 through 8. Verified: those eight sum to the printed total. A leading (1:0) appears on the 2023 sheet and is excluded from the total.

editions.note: The organizer never published results for this edition, nor an answer key. The whole site holds only two 2021 pages, both the call for entries. The cover sheet of the question paper states the contest was answered through an AllCounted web form under auto-scoring (自動計分制) and scored diving-style — best and worst case dropped, 30 of 40 counting — so scores existed but were never posted. The 40 questions are transcribed here from the organizer's own images; the answers come from BaziQA and carry answer_provenance='third-party'.
